question.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+4y=2x.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)$ and ${y}_{2}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$ 

According to the method of variation of parameters, we should seek a particular solution 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}
$$

that satisfies the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=2x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ${u}_{1}(x)=-\int g(x)\,\text{d}x,$ find the function $g.$
question.worked_solution:
We notice that the forcing term is $f(x)=2x.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))^{′}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))^{′}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+2{sin}^{2}⁡(2x) \\  & =2\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent. 

Now, we have the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))}^{′}=2x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-2{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)=2x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to find an integral expression for ${u}_{1}.$ We start by eliminating ${u}_{2}^{′}$ from the second equation:

$$
{u}_{2}^{′}=-\frac{{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & =2x \\ -2{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2(-\frac{{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & =2x \\ -2{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-2{u}_{1}^{′}\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)} & =2x \\ -2{u}_{1}^{′}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)} & =2x \\ -2{u}_{1}^{′}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)} & =2x \\ {u}_{1}^{′} & =-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{1}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int -x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{1} & =-\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$
